chunks.text: Champa/frangipani belongs to the genus Plumeria, in the dogbane family Apocynaceae (subfamily Rauvolfioideae, tribe Plumerieae); the genus honours the French royal botanist Charles Plumier, who explored the tropical Americas and after whom it was named. Plumeria comprises 18 accepted species plus one natural hybrid, and Plumeria alba specifically is native to Puerto Rico and the Lesser Antilles, while the wider genus is native to the Neotropics — Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and northwestern South America. It has since been planted across the tropics worldwide, including Florida, Hawaii, southern China, and northern India, Nepal and Bangladesh. Plumerias are deciduous shrubs or small trees with thick, succulent branches that exude a milky latex sap containing compounds that can irritate skin and eyes. Leaves cluster at the branch tips; P. alba has narrow, corrugated leaves. Flowers bloom from early summer into autumn in five-petalled waxy clusters in white, pink, yellow, red or orange, and are intensely fragrant, especially at night, with scent notes likened to jasmine, citrus, gardenia, coconut, peach or vanilla. Curiously, the flowers produce no nectar at all — sphinx moths are lured to pollinate them purely by deceptive scent and appearance.

Champa/frangipani flowers are widely used in Hindu temple offerings and garlands across India, and in Hawaii they are a staple of lei-making. Indian incense sticks that use plumeria in their scent profile are often labelled 'champa', most famously nag champa, which combines plumeria with sandalwood. In Ayurvedic tradition, plumeria has been used to reduce fever and joint inflammation and as a treatment for colic; extracts of the flowers and latex have also been studied for antifungal and antibacterial properties, and traditional use extends to treating skin conditions, herpes and scabies. In Mesoamerica, the plumeria held deep symbolic importance for over two thousand years among the Maya and Aztec, representing life, fertility and elite status, and Plumeria rubra is today Nicaragua's national flower. In parts of Southeast Asia, by contrast, the tree is associated with death and spirits and is often planted in cemeteries, partly because its fragrance was believed to mask the smell of decay.
